title: When: The Scientific Secrets of Perfect Timing

facts.claim: Pink opens with a Cornell study (Golder and Macy): about 500 million tweets from about 2.4 million users in 84 countries over two years; positive affect rose in the morning, dropped in the afternoon, rose again in the evening - peak, trough, rebound - across continents and time zones.
facts.source: Guardian review via inkl; Time Healthland; Goodreads highlight

facts.claim: Earnings calls study (Chen, Demers, Lev): 26,000+ calls from about 2,100 US firms; afternoon calls were 'more negative, irritable, and combative' than morning calls, and the tone affected stock prices.

For analytic tasks people perform better in the morning (peak); for insight tasks most people (larks and 'third birds') do better in the late afternoon/early evening when their guard is down; Pink calls this the 'inspiration paradox'. Owls are reversed.
facts.source: youexec summary; tedneward notes; Goodreads highlight

facts.claim: Larks and third birds experience the day as peak, trough, rebound; owls in roughly reverse order.

Duke study cited by Pink: about 90,000 surgeries; anesthetic adverse events were significantly more frequent for cases starting in the 3 and 4 p.m. hours: about 1% at 9 a.m. vs 4.2% at 4 p.m.; actual harm 0.3% at 8 a.m. vs 1% at 3 p.m. Researchers: afternoon circadian lows impair physician vigilance.
facts.source: PCMA book excerpt; Duke Health press release; Fool interview

facts.claim: Pink cites University of Pennsylvania research that hand-washing in hospitals deteriorates considerably in the afternoon.

Danish schoolchildren scored worse on standardised tests taken later in the day; a 20-30 minute break 'to eat, play, and chat' before a test raised scores; 'a break causes an improvement that is larger than the hourly deterioration'.

Nappuccino: drink coffee, then nap; caffeine takes about twenty-five minutes to enter the bloodstream; ideal naps are ten to twenty minutes; longer brings sleep inertia; five-minute naps did little, ten-minute naps had effects lasting nearly three hours.
facts.source: Goodreads highlights; tedneward notes; focusu review

facts.claim: Alter and Hershfield: '9-enders' (ages 29, 39, 49...) are overrepresented among first-time marathoners by 48 percent; about half the people in a typical marathon are first-timers.
Alter and Hershfield propose that nearing the end of a decade people do a kind of 'meaning audit' of their lives.
Connie Gersick's study: business students had eleven days for a case analysis; around the midpoint (day six) the groups dropped their weak initial approach and adopted a new strategy.

Berger and Pope: in 18,000+ NBA games, teams trailing by one point at halftime won more often than expected. Pink's advice: at a midpoint say 'uh-oh' and get to work rather than 'oh no' and give up; make midpoints visible.
facts.source: BPS Research Digest; Catalyst Q&A; youexec

facts.claim: Golder and Macy: on weekends the morning mood peak came about two hours later; mood still declined during the day on weekends, so the pattern was not only work-driven.

Pink: Danish break boost equivalent to about three extra weeks in the classroom; a break every hour would make scores rise over the day; restorative breaks: moving over stationary, social over solo, outside over inside.
Duke authors pointed to end-of-day fatigue and afternoon hand-offs; some hospitals added vigilance time-outs (Pink, via summary).
facts.source: Duke Health press release; youexec summary

facts.claim: Midpoints can be a slump or a spark; after the midpoint teams are less open to new ideas but most open to coaching. Halftime effect about half the size of home-court advantage; motivation the proposed cause.
facts.source: tedneward notes; BPS Research Digest; Berger & Pope paper

facts.claim: Alter and Hershfield reported 9-enders ran faster marathons than people two years younger or older.
facts.source: Good Morning America report on PNAS 2014

facts.claim: Later work contested the 9-ender effect (Frontiers in Psychology 2015 commentary found no evidence; a reanalysis found the marathon effect non-significant when whole decades are compared).

rejected.claim: Hemingway's morning routine as Pink's example; 'Pink examined thousands of studies and found Hemingway intuitively right'
rejected.reason: No source puts this in When.

rejected.claim: Prefrontal cortex at full capacity in the morning; late-night second peak
Traffic, medical and industrial accidents concentrated 2-4 p.m.
rejected.reason: Not verified as a book statistic; only anesthesia data verified.

rejected.claim: NASA pilots, Google employees, Japanese firms made naps official policy
'Five minutes and a cup of coffee'
rejected.reason: Book says five-minute naps do little; ten to twenty minutes.

rejected.claim: 29/39/49-year-olds register at nearly double the rate of 28/38/48-year-olds

rejected.reason: Not Pink's term; his midpoint/ending framing differs.

1273.note: Hemingway anecdote rejected; center (time of day changes which work goes well) rebuilt on the tweets study, earnings calls and analytic vs insight. Title changed.

1274.note: Afternoon trough rebuilt on Duke anesthesia data, Danish break study and the nappuccino; unverified accident stats and company nap policies dropped.

1275.note: Marathon figure corrected to 48%; 'last step effect' label dropped; midpoint material (Gersick, halftime) used for the mid-project slump. Title changed.
